data: Skeleton entry for /fleet (PRD-012 v0.2 / Phase A scaffold). Builder + agency + first-flight per public sources. Specs and gallery TBD in later phases.

Mir was the first modular space station — and the bridge between two eras of spaceflight. Where every station before it was launched whole, Mir was assembled in orbit over a decade, module by module, growing into a sprawling complex that stayed aloft for fifteen years. It set the endurance record that still stands (Valeri Polyakov's 437 unbroken days, proof a crew could survive a Mars-length flight), outlived the Soviet Union that built it by a decade, and survived a fire and a depressurising collision in 1997 that its crew fought off by hand. In its final years American Shuttles docked with it and US astronauts lived aboard — the rehearsal, in hardware and in trust, for the International Space Station that inherited nearly everything Mir worked out.

The first modular space station, assembled in orbit between 1986 and 1996 and continuously occupied for almost 10 years (1989–1999), with a final crew visit in April–June 2000. Hosted American astronauts during the Shuttle-Mir program (1995–1998) — the partnership that made ISS possible.
Last Almaz military station — Soyuz 21 + Soyuz 24 crews; Soyuz 23 failed approach; reentered 1977-08-08 after 412 days
Second Almaz military station — Soyuz 14 crew Jul 1974; Soyuz 15 failed automatic docking; reportedly tested an onboard cannon 1975-01-24
Civilian DOS-4 station — hosted Soyuz 17 (29 days) + Soyuz 18 (63 days, then-longest spaceflight) crews; deorbited 1977-02-03
First Almaz military station — depressurised on orbit before any crew arrived; reentered 1973-05-28 after 54 days
